en: The Sūtra on the Seal of the Dharma Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial and Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, under Imperial Edict.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī together with a community of bhikṣus.
Then the Buddha addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know that there is a Seal of the Noble Dharma; I shall now analyze and expound it for you."
"You all should give rise to pure knowledge and vision; listen attentively, receive it with care, attend to it well, and reflect upon it with mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will proclaim it for us; we delight in hearing it.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus! Emptiness is non-existent, free from conceptual construction, without arising, without cessation, and detached from all cognition and views. Why is this?
Emptiness has no location and no form; it is not characterized by perception, is fundamentally unarisen, is beyond the reach of knowledge and vision, and is free from all attachments.
Because of being free from attachment, one encompasses all phenomena and abides in the view of equality; this is the true view.
Bhikṣus, you should know that such is emptiness, and so too are all phenomena; this is called the Seal of the Dharma (dharmamudrā).
"Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
This Dharma-seal is precisely the three gates of liberation; it is the fundamental Dharma of all Buddhas, the eye of all Buddhas, for it is that to which all Buddhas resort."
Therefore, you all should listen attentively, receive this with care, keep it in mind, reflect upon it, and observe it as it truly is. "Furthermore, monks!

If there is a practitioner who goes to the forest, or dwells at the foot of a tree in various secluded places, they should observe as it truly is that form is suffering, empty, and impermanent; they should give rise to revulsion and abide in the vision of equanimity."

Observing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in this way—as suffering, as empty, and as impermanent—one should give rise to weary detachment and abide in the vision of equality.
"O Bhikṣus! All aggregates (skandhas) are fundamentally empty, arising from the mind; once the mental factors have ceased, the aggregates are without activity.
To understand this thus is right liberation. Having attained right liberation, one is free from all cognitions and views; this is called the gate of liberation through emptiness."

"Furthermore, abiding in samādhi, one contemplates that all objective forms are entirely extinguished and one is free from all perceptions of existence; likewise, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are also entirely extinguished and free from all perceptions of existence. To observe in this manner is called the gate of liberation through non-perception."
Having entered this gateway of liberation, one immediately attains pure knowledge and vision.
Because of this purity, greed, hatred, and delusion are all completely extinguished.
Once these have been extinguished, one abides in the vision of equality.

One who abides in this view is immediately free from the view of self and the view of what belongs to self; they thoroughly understand all views, such that nothing arises and there is nothing upon which to rely.
Furthermore, once one is free from the view of self, there is no seeing and no hearing, no perception and no cognition.

Why is this? Because consciousnesses arise by way of causes and conditions; both those causes and conditions and the consciousnesses produced thereby are entirely impermanent. Because they are impermanent, consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Since the aggregate of consciousness is empty and devoid of volitional activity, it is called the gate of liberation through non-action.
Having entered this gate of liberation, one knows the ultimate nature of phenomena, remains unattached to phenomena, and realizes the quiescence of phenomena.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is called the Seal of the Noble Dharma, which is none other than the three gates of liberation.
Bhikṣus, if you cultivate and train yourselves in this, you shall attain pure knowledge and vision."
At that time, having heard this Dharma, all the bhikṣus were filled with great joy; they prostrated themselves, and with faith, accepted it.
Thus ends the Buddha’s *Dharmamudrā Sūtra*.
